plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 16: Chemistry of Benzene: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a reaction energy diagram set inside a pale blue rectangular panel, following benzene and bromine along two competing pathways. A tall arrow at the far left, shaded from pale yellow at the bottom to orange at the top, is labeled "Energy"; the horizontal axis beneath the panel reads "Reaction progress" and ends in a magenta arrow. Reactants sit on a dashed level at the left, drawn as a benzene hexagon, a plus sign, and "Br2" in magenta. A black curve climbs from that level to a high first maximum capped by a short dashed line, with a vertical double-headed arrow between maximum and reactant level labeled delta-G double-dagger. The curve drops into a trough, where a cationic intermediate is drawn as a partly unsaturated six-membered ring bearing an H and a magenta Br on the same carbon with a plus sign above it, then rises to a lower second maximum and falls to a dashed product level below the reactants, where bromobenzene plus "HBr" sit above the word "Substitution"; a small double-headed arrow labeled delta-G degrees spans the reactant-to-product gap. From the same trough a magenta curve branches upward over its own maximum and ends above the reactant level at a bracketed dibrominated ring labeled "Addition" and "(does not occur)". Placing both endpoints on one vertical energy scale is what carries the argument: the substitution branch finishes downhill while the addition branch finishes uphill.

demo_steps.title: Reactants
demo_steps.narration: Benzene and Br₂ begin on a common dashed energy level; everything that happens next plays out on the black curve above them.

demo_steps.title: First barrier
demo_steps.narration: The system climbs the first, tallest peak — the transition state for attacking the aromatic π system. The ΔG‡ arrow spans this full climb.

demo_steps.title: Cationic intermediate
demo_steps.narration: The curve dips into a trough housing the sigma complex: a non-aromatic cation bearing both H and Br on one ring carbon. This is where the addition branch forks off.

demo_steps.title: Second barrier
demo_steps.narration: A second, smaller peak must be crossed — deprotonation of the ring carbon, which restores aromaticity.

demo_steps.title: Substitution products
demo_steps.narration: The black curve falls to bromobenzene + HBr on a level below the reactants: overall ΔG° is downhill, so substitution is thermodynamically favorable.

demo_steps.title: Why addition fails
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the addition pathway: the magenta branch ends on a dibrominated product level above the reactants — uphill ΔG° — so addition does not occur.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: On a single vertical energy scale the competition is decided by the endpoints: substitution loses a proton to restore aromaticity and ends downhill, while addition ends uphill and therefore does not occur.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Pale blue panel containing the full diagram. Vertical Energy arrow on the far left with a yellow-to-orange gradient; horizontal 'Reaction progress' label below with a magenta arrowhead. One black curve with two humps (first taller) and a trough; from the trough a magenta curve branches upward to the addition endpoint. All structures sit in the lower region of the panel, aligned roughly with their energy level: reactants lower-left with 'Br2' in magenta; intermediate cation centered under the trough; substitution products lower-right with 'HBr' in magenta; addition product in the upper-right enclosed in square brackets with magenta '(does not occur)'. Dashed horizontal levels mark reactants and products; a short dashed cap marks the first peak. ΔG‡ is a tall double-headed arrow, ΔG° a short one. Highlighting should light up the active structure plus the corresponding point on the curve, and the chosen pathway's curve and endpoint while dimming the other.

authoredContext:
Why does the reaction of Br2 with benzene take a different course than its reaction with an alkene? The answer is straightforward. If addition occurred, the 150 kJ/mol stabilization energy of the aromatic ring would be lost and the overall reaction would be endergonic. When substitution occurs, though, the stability of the aromatic ring is retained and the reaction is exergonic. An energy diagram for the overall process is shown in the figure.

An energy diagram for the electrophilic bromination of benzene. Because the stability of the aromatic ring is retained, the overall process is exergonic.

Energy diagram shows curve exhibiting two peaks, with the first peak higher than second. A second curve originates from the trough of the first curve and ends higher in energy than the first curve.
